newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo economy could collapse on internal debts.
newsitem.headline: Yugo economy could collapse on internal debts.

text.p: The Yugoslav economy risks collapse under the weight of internal commercial debt which is fast approaching the level of M1 money supply, economists warned on Wednesday.

"Internal debts rose by 5.8 percent to reach 3.988 billion dinars ($819.3 million) at the end of July when M1 money supply stood at 4.34 billion dinars," said Tomislav Milisavljevic of the Belgrade-based Institute for Market Research (IZIT).
According to the latest IZIT figures, there were 20,301 insolvent companies at the end of July -- 7.2 percent more than a month earlier.
Most alarmingly, 93,5 percent of the total were permanently insolvent. Their overdue and unpaid liabilities stood at 3.809 billion dinars.
Slobodan Milosavljevic also of the IZIT said the only possible cure was what he termed "multilateral compensation" in which all debts are cancelled.
"This would annul all internal debts and companies and banks would have a clear way to start from scratch," Milosavljevic told Reuters.
"After getting rid of such a huge burden, companies could turn to new business programmes, but generally it would be just a technical help," he added.
According to Milosavljevic, the same situation happened in the former Yugoslavia at the end of 1970's, when a "general compensation" swept away all debts.
Beside the crippling illiquidity, Serbian and Montenegrin companies face an even more serious problem after 3-1/2 years of U.N. economic sanctions -- an acute shortage of working capital.

"Our economy would need at least $1 billion of foreign capital to begin to breathe," said Milosavljevic. "But it would only help if foreign funds are given strictly to economically viable programmes."
But economists agreed the central bank should not secumb to the temptation to quietly expand money supply.
"The central bank must stick to its advocated monetary aims and print new money only if backed by hard currency," an analyst said.

Despite desperate state of internal debts, economists said it was unlikely any medicine would be offered to the crippled economy before the November 3 elections. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
